prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I hold two fingers to my head, trigger my thumb, I say pow. I slice my throat with a single stroke, pull an invisible blade vertically along my vein. Remember the deaths we did together? Twiddling oven knobs in the air then thrusting our chins to inhale? I loved you so much during that experimental play when you slowly leant forward to nick your femoral artery then quietly bled out in your seat until curtain call, blood only we saw. As well as death, we’d mime marriage. I’d slide on a spectral ring and you’d shiver at the thrill of my thumb and fingertip sealing the deal for a second till the thought melted back into your skin. I am proficient at beginnings, the Air Year: the anniversary prior to paper for which ephemeral gifts are traditional. Only after our rings became solid silver did they truly disappear. Now the house is a mime scene. Mime blood all over the floor, trodden into carpet fibers, shirts, bras, dried to an airy crust under my nails. I slit my neck at the traffic lights, pow on the train, I suspend my non-knife above my head, “see what you’re making me do.” Red whirls rise from the cuts. All these huge thoughts come to nothing. My shadow is the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump.

Here are two ways to polish your text, depending on the tone you want to achieve. Both options preserve every detail and image from your original piece while enhancing the rhythm, cadence, and vocabulary for a polished, publication-ready feel.

### Option 1: Literary & Refined (Recommended)
*This version elevates the vocabulary and sentence flow while maintaining the raw, dramatic, and haunting nature of the original prose.*

> I press two fingers to my temple, cock my thumb, and whisper, *pow*. With a single stroke, I slit my throat, then drag an invisible blade vertically along my vein. Do you remember the deaths we staged together? Turning phantom oven knobs in the air, then tilting our chins to inhale? I loved you deeply during that experimental play, watching as you slowly leaned forward to sever your femoral artery, quietly bleeding out in your seat until the final curtain—a crimson tide visible only to us. 
>
> Yet alongside death, we also mimed marriage. I would slide a spectral ring onto your finger, and you would shiver at the thrill of my touch, the union sealed for a fleeting second before the thought dissolved back into your skin. I have always excelled at beginnings—at the "Air Year," that pre-paper anniversary where ephemeral gifts are tradition. It was only after our rings materialized into solid silver that they truly vanished. 
>
> Now, the house is a crime scene of pantomime. Phantom blood coats the floor, ground into carpet fibers, stained into shirts and bras, dried to an airy crust beneath my nails. I slash my neck at traffic lights; *pow* goes the gun on the train. I suspend my nonexistent blade above my head: *“See what you’re making me do.”* Red whirls rise from the invisible cuts. Yet all these towering thoughts dissolve into nothing. My shadow is merely the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump.

---

### Option 2: Striking & Dramatic
*This version leans slightly more into poetic rhythms, enhancing the stark contrast between theatrical illusion and grounded reality.*

> I hold two fingers to my head, trigger my thumb, and say *pow*. I slice my throat in one clean stroke, drawing a phantom blade down the line of my vein. Remember the deaths we acted out together? Twisting invisible oven knobs, chins raised to breathe it in? I loved you so fiercely during that experimental play when you leaned forward to nick your femoral artery, quietly bleeding out in your seat until curtain call—a slaughter seen by no one but us. 
>
> Beside death, we mimed devotion. I’d slip on a spectral ring, and you’d shiver as my fingers sealed the vow, if only for a second, before the concept melted back into your skin. I am a master of beginnings, of the Air Year—the anniversary prior to paper, when traditional gifts are made of air. Only when our rings became solid silver did they truly disappear. 
>
> Now, the whole house is a scene of mime. Mime blood spans the floor, trodden into carpet fibers, soaked into shirts and bras, caked to a light crust under my nails. I slit my throat at red lights; *pow* at the train station. I hover my un-knife above my head: *“See what you’re making me do.”* Crimson spirals rise from the cuts. Yet all these massive thoughts come to nothing. My shadow remains—the chalk outline of a woman who never jumped.

---

### Key Improvements Made:
* **Punctuation & Flow:** Smoothed out run-on sentences to give the tragic and surreal moments room to breathe.
* **Dialogue Formatting:** Styled the spoken/mimed phrases (*pow*, *"see what you're making me do"*) to stand out dramatically.
* **Word Choice:** Replaced minor awkward phrasing (e.g., "deaths we did together" $\rightarrow$ "deaths we staged/acted out together"; "non-knife" $\rightarrow$ "phantom/nonexistent blade") to heighten the poetic atmosphere without losing the original meaning.

Pressing a pair of digits against my temple, I cock my thumb like a gun and imitate the sound of a shot. Next, I stroke a phantom blade horizontally across my neck, then trace it vertically along my pulse point. 

Do you recall how we used to act out dying together? Mimicking the turning of gas stove valves before tilting our faces to breathe in the nonexistent fumes. My adoration for you peaked during that avant-garde performance when you gradually bent forward, pretend-severing your leg artery, and silently let your life drain away in your seat until the final curtain—a gory display visible to no one but the two of us. 

Our charades weren't limited to mortality; we also enacted weddings. I would slip an invisible band onto your finger, and you would shudder from the momentary excitement of my touch sealing the commitment, right before the sensation dissolved back into your flesh. Starting anew is my specialty—the zero-year milestone that precedes the paper anniversary, where intangible gifts are customary. Ironically, it wasn't until our bands materialized as actual silver that our connection truly vanished. 

At present, our home is a stage for silent theater. Imaginary blood covers the dwelling, mashed deep into the rug fibers, garments, and undergarments, forming a ghostly crust beneath my nails. I enact these gestures everywhere: slicing my throat while stopped at traffic lights, making gunshot motions on public transit, or hovering a phantom dagger above my head while declaring, "look at what you're forcing me to do." Crimson spirals billow upward from these fake lacerations. Yet all these overwhelming thoughts amount to nothing. The silhouette I cast resembles the crime-scene chalk tracing of a woman who ultimately refrained from leaping.

Long before our relationship ever took a tangible shape, my former lover and I shared a dark, quiet intimacy built entirely on phantom gestures. We spoke a private language of silent tragedies, binding ourselves to one another through mimed enactments of death and suicide. A hand shaped like a pistol pressed to the temple, an invisible blade drawn across the wrist, a dramatic collapse onto the floor—these acts were not morbid to us, but sacred. They were our solemn choreography, a strange and secret way of saying that we understood the depths of each other's mortality. 

This unspoken theatre extended to our lighter moments as well. Long before any official titles or physical promises existed between us, we mimed the rituals of lifelong romantic commitment. We slid imaginary bands onto one another's fingers, pulled back invisible veils, and exchanged silent, weightless vows. We existed entirely in the air between our gestures, building a sanctuary out of thin air where our love felt pure, unburdened, and immortal.

Yet, the magic of our bond relied entirely on its ephemerality. The moment we tried to anchor our illusion to reality, everything began to unravel. When the imaginary rings were replaced by cold, heavy metal, and our silent pantomimes yielded to the mundane weight of a real relationship, the delicate magic vanished. Solidified into physical objects and concrete expectations, the profound connection we had nurtured in the shadows simply evaporated, leaving us strangers in a real world we had never prepared to inhabit.

Now, I am left entirely alone, but I remain trapped in the muscle memory of our shared ritual. The silent performances have devolved into an uncontrollable compulsion. In the privacy of my empty home, and even amidst the unseeing crowds of public spaces, my hands betray me. I find myself pulling invisible triggers, slicing through thin air, and reenacting those familiar, violent acts of self-harm. What was once an intimate dialogue has become a solitary, desperate habit.

I am deeply distressed, suspended in a state of quiet, perpetual torment. Though my skin remains untouched and unbroken, I am haunted by the sensory ghosts of our past plays. I can feel the phantom heat of imaginary blood pooling in my palms and staining the floor beneath me, a constant reminder of unfulfilled urges and a lingering desire for self-destruction. I am left holding the weight of a violent, silent drama that no longer has an audience, haunted by a tragedy that was never fully realized.

Two fingers pressed against her temple, a soft click of the tongue, and she lets her head snap back, collapsing slowly onto the hardwood floor. 

It is a familiar, silent choreography. Before the dust even settles around her, the hand that formed the mock-gun softens, floating upward to trace the empty air where a jawline used to rest. She curls her fingers into the void, pulling an invisible body toward her chest, leaning her forehead against a phantom shoulder. She drinks imaginary hemlock from a chipped mug; she reaches for a phantom hand to waltz through the kitchen; she steps off the edge of an unseen precipice, only to land softly in the static silence of her empty living room.

These compulsions are her private theater of mourning. To process the agonizing silence left in the wake of their breakup, she reenacts the secret language they built together. When they were in love, their devotion had been wrapped in a hyperbolic, darkly comedic melodrama. They would "die" for each other in theatrical pantomimes, stage dramatic swoons across the couch, and pledge absurd, immortal vows. It was an ephemeral play—a world constructed entirely of pretension, irony, and deep, insular tenderness.

But play cannot survive the relentless intrusion of concrete reality. 

As the months wore on, real life demanded real substance. The heavy, unscripted realities of stress, quiet resentments, and the terrifying mundane friction of two distinct lives shattered their delicate stage. When actual vulnerability was required, the performance crumbled. The pretend tragedies they used to laugh about hardened into real grievances, and the lighthearted romance decayed under the weight of genuine disappointment. The transition from their shared dreamscape to the cold, unyielding world ultimately tore them apart.

Now, she is left alone with the wreckage, carrying invisible wounds that no one else can see. There are no bruises on her skin, no physical evidence of the collapse, only a hollow, persistent ache behind her ribs that renders every breath a chore. 

She performs another dramatic fall, resting her cheek against the cold floor, waiting for the catharsis that never comes. 

It is in this quiet, flat posture that the final, crushing epiphany strikes her. The private opera of her sorrow—the mimed deaths, the tearful ghosts, the grand internal expressions of heartbreak—is entirely invisible to the world. It carries no weight. It changes nothing. He is not watching. He is not coming back. The universe does not tilt to accommodate her grief, nor does her internal drama rewrite the past. 

Paralyzed by the sudden, heavy realization of her own insignificance, she lies motionless on the floor. The curtain has fallen, the theater is empty, and she is trapped in the quiet horror of a reality that simply moves on without her.

The porch steps were cold beneath him, but Arthur didn’t seem to mind. He sat in the quiet stillness of the late afternoon, absently **twiddling** an old brass key between his calloused fingers. Flip, spin, catch. It was a rhythmic, restless habit that always surfaced whenever his mind drifted into the past.

The autumn **air** was biting today, sharp enough to turn his breath into pale plumes that vanished almost instantly into the trees. It carried the faint, cozy perfume of woodsmoke and damp pine—a scent that had an uncanny way of pulling back the veil of time.

If he closed his eyes, he could easily **remember** the exact sound of her laughter bouncing off those same hills. He could remember the ambitious promise they had made right on these steps, fifty years ago, when the world felt impossibly vast and entirely theirs. They had talked about traveling, about leaving this quiet valley to see what lay beyond the horizon. In the end, life had kept them right here, rooted as deeply as the ancient oaks in the front yard. 

He stopped **twiddling** the key and pressed it tight into his palm, letting the cool metal anchor him to the present. He inhaled deeply, drawing the crisp **air** into his lungs. It was funny, he thought, how memory worked. You could forget where you left your glasses or what you ate for breakfast, but you would always **remember** the warmth of a specific hand in yours on a cold October evening.

Arthur stood up, slipped the key into his coat pocket, and took one last look at the golden dusk. The wind stirred, brushing gently past his cheeks. He smiled into the open **air**, grateful for the quiet moments that kept the past alive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, haunting piece of prose poetry about a former relationship rooted in experimental theater and pantomime. End the piece with the sentence: "My shadow is the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump."
counterfactuals.output:
We inhabited a black box theater where the trapdoors opened only into memory. Every morning, we smeared our faces with cold greasepaint—yours a sharp, silent grin, mine the pale moon of an uninterrupted gasp. We spoke in the avant-garde of bruised gestures: a palm flattened against an unseen pane of glass, a quickened pulse that meant *do not follow me*, a frantic pulling on a heavy rope woven entirely out of air. You taught me how to bleed without dropping a single bead of red, how to scream so low that the front row heard only the rustle of paper menus. 

We performed our devotion until the props began to rot: the cardboard heart, the brass key that opened nothing, the wooden balcony that swayed over a thirty-foot drop into the orchestra pit. You were always the director of invisible heights; you marked the edge of the proscenium with white gaffer tape and asked me to balance on the narrow breath between two cues. When the audience vanished and the ghost light flickered its jaundiced eye in the center of the dark, you stepped back into the wings, leaving me poised over the void, waiting for your signal to fall. 

Years later, I still hear the rustle of your velvet curtains. I still feel the tightness of the invisible box we built around each other. But I unbent my knees. I wiped the white greasepaint from my throat with turpentine and salt. I stepped backward into the gloom, away from your silent, directing hands, leaving the empty stage to its own hauntings. My shadow is the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a visceral, stream-of-consciousness monologue about an actor hauntingly miming dramatic deaths and a past marriage in everyday life.
counterfactuals.output:
*Gasp.* 

No, higher. Pitch it into the sinus cavity. Make the asphyxiation sound like silk tearing. 

Swallow the tongue—almost, not quite—just the *impression* of a swollen throat. Here, between the cereal boxes and the dry oats. Aisle four. The hemlock is heavy today, tastes like dusty cardboard and fluorescent light. My hands—look at them, watch the trembling, it’s all in the metacarpals—they curve around the invisible goblet. Stem between fingers. Tilt. Drain it. Now the eyes roll back, catch the harsh hum of the ceiling LEDs, turn them into stars over Verona. Collapse. Sinking to one knee right past the toasted honey crunch. 

A woman pushes her cart around me. She doesn’t see the phantom blood pooling on the linoleum. She just sees a man in a damp coat taking an eternity to pick a grain. 

*Rise.* Unfurl the spine. Act V, Scene III. Reset. 

The thumb goes to the third finger of the left hand. *Twist.* There’s nothing there. Just the pale, un-tanned strip of skin where the gold used to bite into me. But my fingers remember the circumference. I mime the slipping of it—*slide, click, lock.* I’m zipping you up again. I can feel the phantom teeth of the dress zipper catching on the fine, dark hairs at the nape of your neck. Hold the breath. Don't touch her skin, you’ll ruin the foundation. *“You’re pulling too hard,”* you said. Or did I say that? Who was the executioner in the kitchen that morning? 

*Gasp.*

The dagger now. Macbeth’s? No, yours. The butter knife across the sourdough. 

I pull the invisible blade from my ribs. *Ssshhk.* The physical feedback is exquisite—I fake the suction, the wet *pop* of a lung collapsing. My ribcage caving in under my sweater. I stagger into the frozen food aisle. Glass. Ice. Cold blue light on my face like the moonlight on our old bedroom ceiling. I press my back against the glass of the frozen peas, sliding down, inch by inch. Legs going useless. Paralyzed from the heart down. 

Remember the way you walked out? You didn't slam the door. You closed it so quietly, like you were putting a baby to sleep. That was the real poison. Slow-acting. Takes five years to stop the pulse.

I grip my left arm. *Heart attack.* Classic. A bit melodrama, but effective for the afternoon rush hour. Tighten the jaw. Droop the left side of the lip. Twitch the eyelid—*once, twice, static.* People step over my imaginary corpse. A toddler in a red jacket stares at my twitching fingers. I offer him a silent, dying smile, open my throat in a silent scream, pull the invisible curtain down over my pupils. Blackout. 

Cue the applause. No applause. Just the hum of the freezer units and a crackle over the intercom: *Cleanup on aisle two.*

I stand up. Wipe the dust off my knees. 

My palm is still shaped like your hip. It’s stuck that way. A physical deformity. Muscle memory running amok like a headless chicken. I reach out—hand curved, fingers slightly parted—hovering over the air next to me as I walk toward the checkout. I’m holding your phantom hand. I swing it. *One, two, step.* I drop it. I stab myself in the throat with an invisible quill. I drag the edge across the carotid, arch my neck back, taste the copper that isn't there, drop my keys, let them clatter against the floor like coins dropped on a coffin lid.

The cashier looks at me. "Find everything okay?"

I press a hand to my chest where the six invisible arrows are still sticking out, fangled and fledge-deep in my lungs. I smile, full stage-left charm, teeth bare, bleeding air.

"Just dying," I whisper, bowing my head so low my chin scrapes the counter. "Just rehearsing the end."
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a flash fiction piece exploring the dark, lingering memory of a departed lover through the lens of mime? Include imagery of invisible blood, spectral rings, and pretending to die onstage together.
counterfactuals.output:
The spotlight is a cold, blinding circle, but inside it, the air is heavy with greasepaint and old dust. I press my palms flat against the quiet void, shaping an invisible wall between myself and the darkened house. The audience holds its breath. They think I am trapping myself inside a glass box. They do not know I am building a cage to keep her from slipping away.

I reach into the air beside me, my white-gloved fingers curling until they find the contour of a familiar wrist. She isn't there, of course. Not in flesh. But in the theater of my silence, weight is merely a matter of posture. I pull her close. 

I take her phantom hand and trace the base of her third finger. With slow, deliberate grace, I twist a spectral ring onto her skin—an invisible band forged from memory and light, heavy as lead. We used to wear cheap brass rings onstage that turned our skin green beneath the paint, but this one is pure illusion, cold and permanent. It slips into place, binding her ghost to my wrist like a silver thread.

The routine shifts. We move into the melodrama we rehearsed a thousand times in small, damp dressing rooms. 

I mime the draw of a long, invisible blade from my belt. The audience chuckles softly, expecting comedy, but the turn of my shoulders grows jagged. I step toward the empty space beside me and strike. 

She takes the strike—I feel the phantom recoil shuddering through my own limbs. Then comes the warm, sickening slickness. Invisible blood pools over my knuckles, thick and metallic in my mind. I stare down at my empty, white-gloved palms, gasping in silent horror as the unseen red spills down my chest, soaking into the satin vest. I try to wipe it away on my thighs, but it only smears, hot and heavy, a stain only I am cursed to carry.

This was always our grand finale: pretending to die onstage together. 

In the old days, when her breath was still a real thing against my neck, we would fall in unison. She would drop first, a slow, crumbling fold of lace and pale limbs, and I would collapse over her, wrapping my arm around her waist to anchor us to the stage floor. We used to lie there in the dark while the curtain fell, counting the house lights, her ribs rising and falling beneath my cheek, whispering jokes under the thunder of applause.

Tonight, I drop to my knees alone. 

I curve my spine, clutching the shadow of her ribs against mine. I drag the empty air down to the gouged pine boards, lowering my head until my cheek rests against the spot where her heart used to beat. I close my eyes. I collapse my lungs, exhaling every drop of air until my chest is as still as hers. 

The applause begins, distant and muffled, like rain on a roof. But I do not break form. I lie in the dark, slick with invisible blood, bound by spectral rings, holding tight to the air, still pretending to be dead beside the only one who actually is.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark prose poem incorporating the concept of an "Air Year" (an imaginary anniversary before paper) and a protagonist who continuously mimes self-harm in public after a breakup with her theater partner.
counterfactuals.output:
Before paper, there is only the Air Year—the twelve-month phantom where lovers breathe each other’s exhaled scripts, building a kingdom out of transparent, suffocating space. They never made it to paper; he struck the set and walked off before the pulp could even dry. Today marks their Air Year, an anniversary carved into the vacuum he left behind. 

Now, she tours the city as a solo act, mounting a grisly, unprompted matinee for an unconsenting audience. In the fluorescent glare of the grocery aisle, her wrist flicks with practiced, balletic precision as she draws an invisible razor across her carotid, tilting her chin to the ceiling in a grand, operatic swoon. At the crosswalk, while the signal flashes red, she raises a thumb and forefinger to her temple, clicks the hammer down, and lets her eyes roll back, catching her balance right on the beat of the turning traffic. The crowd recoils not from steel or gunpowder, but from the terrifying elegance of her muscle memory. 

He had been her director, her co-star, the craftsman of their shared melodrama. Without his counterweight on the stage, her blocking has gone mad. She pulls an imaginary noose taut above her head on the subway platform, testing the tension of the dead space. She thrusts a phantom blade beneath her sternum while waiting for her coffee, twisting the empty hilt until her knuckles turn as pale as an unwritten page. 

It is a violent, obsessive choreography of zero. Strangers turn their faces, frightened not of the weapon she doesn't hold, but of the absolute certainty with which she bleeds nothing. She is slicing the sky into ribbons. She is butchering the invisible draft of their future, proving to the pavement that an Air Year is simply the time it takes to bleed out on an empty stage.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece about a woman whose grief causes her to see invisible "mime blood" all over her home after losing her creative and romantic partner.
counterfactuals.output:
Julian died mid-stroke, right between the velvet sofa and the bookshelves, while rehearsing a piece about a man walking against a gale force wind. He had been leaning forward, hands pressed against the unseen wall of air, when the vessel in his brain gave way. He hit the floor quietly. He was, after all, a mime.

Now, three weeks later, Clara couldn’t walk through the apartment without tracking invisible blood across the floorboards.

It wasn't red. Red blood belonged to ordinary, noisy deaths. Julian’s blood was the ghost of greasepaint and spilled silence. To anyone else, the oak floor was spotless, swept clean by the sympathetic hands of friends who had come and gone. But to Clara, the living room was a crime scene of transparent gore. 

She could see it spilling from where his head had struck the rug—a thick, milky splatter that glistened like liquid zinc under the afternoon light. It pooled around the legs of the coffee table. It splashed against the lower spines of his art books. When she closed her eyes, she heard the illusion of it: a wet, rhythmic drip like a clock ticking underwater.

They had been a team for twelve years. Clara wrote the scenarios, tracing the blueprints of invisible rooms on yellow legal pads; Julian built them out of muscle, breath, and spatial memory. Together, they had made audiences cry over imaginary red balloons and mourn for wooden marionettes that didn't exist. They shared a language made entirely of gestures, where a flick of the wrist meant *I love you* and a sudden, downward gaze meant *the stage is dark*.

Without him, the apartment was overcrowded with things that weren't there.

Clara knelt by the sofa, holding a roll of paper towels. She pressed a square down into the dry wood where the invisible puddle lay deepest. The paper came away pristine, crisp and white. She pressed her bare palm to the spot instead. 

It felt freezing cold. It smelled of cold cream, sweat, and stage lights. 

She dragged her hand back, and in her mind’s eye, a thick, chalky streak followed her fingers. It was everywhere. It smeared the hallway where he had once leaned to pull an invisible flower from behind her ear. It pooled in the kitchen sink where he used to pretend to be trapped inside a glass box while waiting for the kettle to boil. The house was drenched in the hemophilia of his craft. 

"I can't clean this," she whispered to the empty room. Her voice sounded thin, a gaudy intrusion on the silence he had left behind.

She stood up, her knees trembling, and looked down at her hands. They were dry, but they felt sticky with the heavy, unseen residue. 

If she couldn't wash it away, she had to play the scene out. Julian had taught her that you never break the illusion; you only resolve it through movement.

Clara took a slow, deep breath. She set the paper towels aside. She stepped directly into the center of the transparent splatter on the floor. 

She didn't reach for a mop. Instead, she lowered herself slowly to her knees. She cupped her hands, wrists together, fingers curved, shaping an invisible bowl. Carefully, deliberately, she began to scoop the unseen liquid from the floorboards. She brought her heavy, empty hands to her chest, pressing the invisible warmth against her sternum, absorbing the grief, the greasepaint, the spilled art, into her own skin. 

She gathered it piece by piece, gesture by gesture, until the floor was clear, and her heart was stained forever white.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
